subject: biology
title: Base Pairs & Population Data
welcome_lead: Today you'll crack the DNA code — the rules that pair the bases A-T and C-G — and read data tables showing how traits vary in real populations.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology DNA base pairing — complementary strands (A-T, C-G), interpreting variation data tables.
final_note: You learned that A pairs with T, C pairs with G, how to write a complementary strand, and how to read variation data from a population.

concepts.def: Letter of the DNA code: A, T, C or G
Two bases joined across the helix (A-T or C-G)
The opposite DNA strand built using base pair rules
Base that always pairs with thymine (T)
Base that always pairs with guanine (G)
How common a trait is within a population

walkthroughs.body_html:
DNA has only 4 letters: A, T, C, G.

They're called bases. Their order spells the genetic message.

The two strands hold hands using strict rules:

A always pairs with T · C always pairs with G.

So if one strand reads A-T-C-G, the other must read T-A-G-C. Easy!

Surveys count traits in real populations — eye colour, height, blood group.

Look for the most common trait and the spread. Continuous traits (height) form a curve; discrete traits (blood group) form bars.

numericals.q: A DNA sample has 30% adenine (A). What percentage of the bases will be thymine (T)?
numericals.hint: A always pairs 1-to-1 with T, so the percentages match
